title: What strategy does—and who makes it
summary: Connect purpose, competitive advantage and the choices made at corporate, business and functional levels.
takeaway: A strategy gives connected decisions a direction; its levels must reinforce each other.
notes: The original growth-strategy row says “makes no change”; that describes stability rather than growth. The wording is retained below as a source discrepancy, not a definition to follow.
The attributed definitions are quotations in the supplied notes; their original editions and page references were not supplied.

title: Strategic management: analysis to action
summary: Follow strategic analysis, formulation, implementation and evaluation as a continuing management cycle.
takeaway: Review the environment and your resources together, then revisit decisions as evidence changes.

ranges.heading: Why strategy needs a management cycle
Questions for position, choices and action

title: Strategy perspectives: planned, emergent and adaptive
summary: Compare strategy lenses, intended and emergent approaches, and market-led versus resource-led thinking.
takeaway: Different perspectives reveal different assumptions; use them together rather than treating one as universally correct.

ranges.heading: Four perspectives and four strategy lenses

notes: The notes describe resource-led strategy as more certain and market-led strategy as riskier. Treat this as a teaching contrast, not a general risk ranking.
Several outside-in/inside-out comparisons are deliberately polarized; actual organizations can combine both approaches.

title: Strategic thinking: logic, creativity and competing demands
summary: Explore analytical and generative reasoning, and ways to manage the tension between market demands and organizational strengths.
takeaway: Use rigorous analysis to test ideas and creative thinking to discover options analysis alone may miss.

title: Strategic business units and accountability
summary: Understand why companies organize distinct businesses around markets, capabilities and responsibility for results.
takeaway: Define the unit before choosing its strategy or assessing its performance.

title: Strategic audit: establish where the business stands
summary: Bring resources, market position and environmental evidence into a focused strategic review.
takeaway: An audit should support a decision; agree its scope, evidence and review date before collecting lists.

ranges.heading: Audit purpose, tools and practical constraints

title: Understanding your competitive landscape
summary: Distinguish market structures and four levels of competition, then examine who competes for the same customer need or budget.
takeaway: Your competitors include alternative ways of meeting a need, not just similar brands.

ranges.heading: Market structures and levels of competition

notes: The four market structures are listed in the source without definitions; this page preserves that list and does not invent missing course explanations.

title: Competitive dynamics: moves, timing and responses
summary: Consider competitive rivalry, likely reactions, and the trade-offs facing first, second and late movers.
takeaway: A move changes the choices available to rivals; assess likely responses before acting.
notes: First-, second- and late-mover outcomes are possibilities, not guaranteed profit or risk rankings.

title: Cost, differentiation and focused strategies
summary: Compare generic strategies, niche positioning, hybrid approaches and the risks of losing a clear basis of advantage.
takeaway: Connect the promised customer benefit to a cost structure the business can sustain.

ranges.heading: Generic strategy, hybrid choices and the strategy clock
Focused strategies and the risks of each position
Hybrid approaches: AirAsia and Lexus examples

notes: The AirAsia, Lexus and IKEA examples are historical teaching illustrations. The notes do not establish their current operations.

title: Market leaders, challengers and followers
summary: Explore market expansion, defensive moves, challenger attacks and follower approaches.
takeaway: Choose actions in the context of your market role, resources and likely response.
notes: Counterfeiting is retained as a named source classification, not recommended business conduct.

title: Strategic groups: map the closest competitors
summary: Map firms by scope and resource commitment to reveal direct rivals, strategic spaces and mobility barriers.
takeaway: Use independent, meaningful axes; proximity on the map should reflect how firms actually compete.

ranges.heading: Mapping groups, strategic spaces and buyers

notes: The automobile map is a historical teaching example, not a current classification of brands or ownership.
The “Strategic Customers” subsection lists search directions without explaining a customer-analysis method; no missing method has been invented.

title: Environmental scanning: from signals to implications
summary: Separate the macro environment, industry relationships and internal conditions, then connect change to managerial tasks.
takeaway: Scanning is useful when signals reach decision-makers and lead to a considered response.

ranges.heading: Layers of the environment and organizational responses

title: PESTLE: assess the wider business environment
summary: Examine political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental influences using the collection’s detailed prompts.
takeaway: Translate external factors into specific opportunities, constraints and actions for the business.
notes: Market/non-market tags in the notes are a simplified teaching distinction; factors can interact across these categories.
Examples involving laws, economies or technologies are prompts from the notes, not current jurisdiction-specific guidance.

title: Porter’s Five Forces: assess industry pressure
summary: Examine rivalry, buyers, suppliers, entry and substitutes, with detailed indicators, applications and limitations.
takeaway: Define the relevant market before judging each force and its implications for profitability.
notes: The source’s positioning responses are possible actions to evaluate, not guarantees that price cuts or acquisitions improve results.

title: Ohmae’s three Cs: company, customer and competitor
summary: Balance organizational strengths, customer needs and competitor offerings when developing a strategic position.
takeaway: A strong position needs all three perspectives, rather than an isolated focus on the company.

ranges.heading: The three perspectives and an application

title: TAM, SAM and SOM: define the market you can serve
summary: Distinguish the total market, the serviceable market and the share realistically obtainable with available resources.
takeaway: Keep the market universe, serviceable scope and obtainable share separate.
notes: The source uses short questions rather than a calculation method; no market estimates or numerical assumptions have been invented.

title: Resources: tangible assets, relationships and capabilities
summary: Distinguish physical and financial resources from relationships, reputation, knowledge, capabilities and attitudes.
takeaway: An asset inventory is a starting point; advantage depends on how resources work together.

title: Core competencies: build strengths that travel
summary: Explore how skills and technologies combine into customer benefits, why capabilities can become rigidities, and how to share strengths across units.
takeaway: A competence is an integrated ability, not simply an asset the business owns.

ranges.heading: Meaning, origins and tests of core competence

notes: The source says core competencies do not depreciate, while also warning of core rigidities. Durability is conditional; capabilities can lose relevance.
Company examples illustrate the notes’ reasoning and are not verified current capability assessments.

title: VRIO and VRIN: evaluate resources and advantage
summary: Assess value, rarity, imitation difficulty and organizational support, while distinguishing the related non-substitutability test.
takeaway: Owning a useful resource is different from being organized to capture its value.

ranges.heading: The VRIO questions and review prompts
Sustainable advantage and the related VRIN criteria

notes: The source mixes VRIO with VRIN: non-substitutability is retained as a related criterion, not relabeled as the O in VRIO.

title: Dynamic capabilities: sense, seize and transform
summary: Understand capability renewal through organizational processes, assets, learning, reconfiguration and path dependence.
takeaway: Capabilities that run today’s business may differ from those needed to change it.

title: Critical success factors: what an industry demands
summary: Explore customer-valued and cost-critical requirements, with technology, manufacturing, distribution, marketing and workforce examples.
takeaway: Distinguish prerequisites for competing from strengths that make your business distinctive.

title: Value chains, networks and outsourcing
summary: Trace primary and support activities, inter-firm relationships, profit pools and make-or-buy choices.
takeaway: Look at the links between activities as well as the activities themselves.
notes: The source says never outsource core activities. Retain this as a strategic caution about losing critical capabilities, rather than an absolute rule for every business.

title: Supply-chain response: mobilize to operate
summary: Follow the five-stage response sequence attributed in the notes to Accenture.
takeaway: Connect risk sensing to scenarios, network configuration, operating action and measurement.
notes: The source labels this “Value Chain Analysis – Accenture”, but its content concerns supply-chain disruption response. Original publication details were not supplied.

title: Ansoff: choose a direction for growth
summary: Compare market penetration, product development, market development and diversification, including constraints and risks.
takeaway: Growth choices change products, markets or both; identify which capabilities and risks change with them.

ranges.heading: Market development and a campaign caution

notes: The “Samsung Galaxy 7” wording and the Burger King campaign are retained as historical source examples with incomplete or potentially inaccurate naming. They are not current factual case studies.
The image suggests a fixed sequence for growth choices. Treat sequencing as the source’s recommendation, not a universal requirement.

title: Diversification and integration: extending business scope
summary: Explore related and unrelated diversification, horizontal and vertical integration, benefits, costs and acquisition examples.
takeaway: Evaluate whether the new scope creates value after coordination costs and capability gaps.

ranges.heading: Integration types, diversification and source examples

notes: Company holdings, transaction dates and prices are unverified historical notes. Preserve them as source claims, not current facts.
The airline integration diagram mixes alliances with integration and uses historical entities; its original relationships are transcribed with that limitation.
The diversification–performance curve is conceptual and supplies no data or estimated optimum.

title: Build, buy or partner: methods for pursuing strategy
summary: Compare organic development with acquisitions, alliances and other ways to pursue strategic choices.
takeaway: Choosing a direction and choosing a delivery method are separate decisions.

ranges.heading: Organic development and the strategic choices menu

title: Blue Ocean Strategy: rethink buyer value
summary: Compare red and blue oceans, explore six search paths and connect cost reduction with increased buyer value.
takeaway: Value innovation asks what can change in the offering and activity system, not merely how to outspend rivals.

ranges.heading: Finding new market space and teaching examples
Value innovation and the strategy canvas

notes: The strategy-canvas image in the source is a rendering-error message. No recoverable plotted values are present; a numerical canvas cannot be reconstructed.
The AirAsia and QB House material is retained as teaching examples, not current operating descriptions.

title: Lean Startup: learn before committing at scale
summary: Connect minimum viable products, build–measure–learn loops, evidence and staged funding.
takeaway: Make progress visible through learning that can support a pivot, perseverance or a stop decision.

ranges.heading: Teams, validated learning and executive decisions

title: Three Horizons: balance today and tomorrow
summary: Distinguish the core business, emerging opportunities and future ideas when planning a growth portfolio.
takeaway: Keep attention on current performance while making room for opportunities at different stages.

title: CAGE: compare international market distance
summary: Examine cultural, administrative, geographic and economic differences before transferring a strategy across countries.
takeaway: Compare specific country pairs and business requirements; distance is more than physical separation.
notes: The China–India comparison contains undated generalizations and historical infrastructure or political assessments. It is preserved as source material, not a current country ranking.
The GE section’s “Alternative and International Market Segmentation” heading has no explanatory text; it is recorded as an incomplete source entry.

title: BCG matrix: balance growth and relative share
summary: Compare stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs, with investment options and the limitations of portfolio analysis.
takeaway: Use the matrix to frame resource-allocation questions, not to make automatic divestment decisions.
notes: The source image labels relative share with a percent sign while its ticks are ratios such as 2×. The recreated visual uses relative-share ratios.
The assertion that profitability is directly determined by relative share is a simplifying source assumption, not a guaranteed relationship.

title: GE matrix: weigh attractiveness against business strength
summary: Use multiple market and business factors to compare portfolio positions and possible investment directions.
takeaway: Make factor definitions and judgments explicit; a nine-cell grid does not remove uncertainty.

ranges.heading: Benefits, market attractiveness and business strength

notes: The source names alternative/international market segmentation without explaining it. No missing method has been invented.
The sample bubbles lack numerical inputs; their positioning is illustrative, not a reproducible company valuation.

title: Gap analysis: turn a desired future into action
summary: Compare the present state with a target, prioritize gaps and consider unexploited strategic spaces.
takeaway: A useful gap has a defined starting point, target and action to close it.

ranges.heading: Closing performance gaps and identifying opportunities

title: Risk management: prioritize uncertainty and response
summary: Identify risks, assess probability and impact, prioritize responses and revisit changing conditions.
takeaway: A risk register should inform choices and resource allocation rather than become a static list.

title: Evaluate strategy: suitability, acceptability and feasibility
summary: Test strategic fit, stakeholder expectations and the practical ability to deliver, with detailed questions and funding considerations.
takeaway: A strategically attractive option still needs acceptable outcomes and a credible delivery plan.

ranges.heading: Suitability: strategic position and analytical tools
Suitability across directions and delivery methods
Acceptability: risk, return and stakeholder reactions
Feasibility: funding, people and operating systems

notes: “SAFe” here means suitability, acceptability and feasibility; it is not the Scaled Agile Framework.
Life-cycle funding, dividends and risk labels are simplified teaching patterns rather than financing prescriptions.

title: Scenario planning: prepare for several futures
summary: Define a planning horizon, explore trends, build scenarios and identify external flags and internal triggers.
takeaway: Scenarios support learning and contingent choices; they are not predictions with invented certainty.

title: SWOT: build an evidence-based strategic diagnosis
summary: Use detailed strength, weakness, opportunity and threat prompts, with benchmarking and common failure modes.
takeaway: SWOT should summarize prior analysis and lead to prioritized choices—not replace evidence gathering.

ranges.heading: Using SWOT and avoiding common failures

title: TOWS: turn SWOT findings into strategic options
summary: Connect internal and external findings using SO, ST, WO and WT options, with the supplied gym and pizza examples.
takeaway: Make each proposed action traceable to the findings it addresses.
notes: Some example cross-references appear inconsistent: for example Domino’s S1+O1 mentions brand while S1 is franchise economics. The original pairings are retained and flagged rather than silently reassigned.
The company diagnoses are undated source exercises, not verified judgments about those businesses today.
The lower portion of the source TOWS image is cropped; visible text is preserved, with the missing endings explicitly marked.

title: Balanced scorecard: connect strategy to measures
summary: Link financial, customer, internal-process and learning objectives with indicators and initiatives.
takeaway: Choose measures that reflect the strategy, and distinguish objectives, targets, indicators and actions.
notes: The retail example proposes replacing staff as a learning-and-growth goal. This is retained as a source example, not endorsed as a development measure.

title: EOS: connect vision, accountability and execution
summary: Explore the six components, meeting cadence, vision planning, quarterly priorities and the source’s toolbox inventory.
takeaway: Connect longer-term direction with measurable priorities, issue solving and a repeatable review cadence.
notes: Several toolbox entries are names only, including LMA, GWC, 5-5-5, Kolbe and the assistance track. They remain explicitly undeveloped source entries.
EOS terminology and tools belong to their respective owners; this educational guide is not an official implementation manual.

title: Build a high-performance team and culture
summary: Connect shared vision, belonging, behavior, resources, clear roles, communication and leadership.
takeaway: Team performance depends on both the conditions for collaboration and the clarity to deliver results.

ranges.heading: Shared vision, organizational conditions and culture

notes: The quotations and their attributions are preserved as supplied; original publication references were not provided.

title: McKinsey 7S: check organizational alignment
summary: Review strategy, structure, systems, skills, style, staff and shared values as connected elements.
takeaway: Changing strategy may require changes in people, systems and organizational design.

title: Kotter: build support and sustain change
summary: Follow the source’s eight-step change sequence from urgency and coalition to sustained organizational practice.
takeaway: A change initiative needs participation, visible progress and reinforcement over time.
notes: This page retains the traditional eight-step wording supplied in the notes. The official methodology has evolved; the further-reading link explains its current presentation.

title: Responding to change: emotion, engagement and support
summary: Separate the emotional stages listed as SARAH from the accompanying empower, engage and equip prompts.
takeaway: Use emotional-response models as prompts for listening, not as a fixed sequence everyone must follow.
notes: The PwC attribution and the connection between SARAH and the sustainability prompts are not established by the source. They are kept separate in the presentation.

title: PROMISE: examine people and culture in integration
summary: Explore development, rewards, leadership, systems, innovation, strategic direction and employee experience across organizations.
takeaway: Integration decisions need attention to how people actually work, not only to structural fit.
notes: The notes do not identify an original author or publication for this PROMISE framework. It is presented as the collection’s integration checklist.

title: Digital maturity: assess more than technology
summary: Consider culture, customers, strategy, technology and operations when reviewing digital transformation.
takeaway: Technology adoption alone does not establish organizational maturity.
notes: The notes attribute the model to Deloitte but provide no scoring rubric, maturity levels or source edition; no assessment score has been invented.

title: Stakeholders: interests, influence and responsibility
summary: Understand stakeholder relationships through descriptive, instrumental and normative perspectives.
takeaway: Identify whose interests and expectations a strategic decision affects.

ranges.heading: The stakeholder model and its perspectives

notes: The three perspectives are named but not developed in the source. This short guide identifies that limit.

title: Customer feedback: NPS labels and service scorecards
summary: Distinguish customer recommendation labels from service ratings, then connect feedback to action.
takeaway: Know what a feedback measure represents before interpreting a score or deciding what to change.
notes: The earlier source names NPS without a survey scale. The accounting collection supplies its percentage-point calculation; question wording and rating thresholds are still not supplied.

editorialSections.heading: From feedback to improvement
paragraphs: Recommendation labels and service ratings answer different questions. The detailed source labels and scorecard below illustrate these measures without supplying a complete survey method. Individual coaching, team huddles and systemic improvement are explained in the related feedback-learning guide.

title: Distributive negotiation: targets, limits and concessions
summary: Prepare target and resistance points, assess the other party’s position and plan concessions.
takeaway: Understand your limits before bargaining over a finite allocation.
notes: “Enlarge the pie” appears in the distributive notes but belongs to value-creation thinking; it is identified as a complementary move rather than the defining distributive mechanism.

title: Principled negotiation: interests, options and BATNA
summary: Combine the overlapping Harvard and principled-negotiation notes while preserving their distinct prompts.
takeaway: Separate people from the problem and compare possible agreements with your best available alternative.

title: Negotiation strategy: avoid common traps
summary: Review preparation, cultural differences, anchoring, leverage, team alignment and implementation risks.
takeaway: Negotiate the whole agreement, including non-price terms and the work needed after agreement.

title: Negotiation from preparation to follow-through
summary: Compare the RADPAC relationship sequence with a practical preparation, bargaining and evaluation process.
takeaway: Closing an agreement is followed by implementation and learning, not the end of the work.
notes: The source introduction describes organizational change rather than negotiation. It is preserved as a mislabeled sentence and excluded from the recommended process.

title: Personal productivity: capture tasks and build habits
summary: Explore the two-minute rule, GTD, a daily habit chain, Parkinson’s Law and the big-rocks approach.
takeaway: Use a reliable task system and protect time for important work; no single rule fits every task.

ranges.heading: Quick tasks and Getting Things Done
Big rocks and the pickle-jar metaphor

notes: The habit-chain attribution to Jerry Seinfeld is supplied without an original reference.
Parkinson’s Law is a heuristic; less time does not automatically mean better results.

title: Kanban: visualize work and limit work in progress
summary: Use a visible workflow, work-in-progress limits, flow management and continuous improvement.
takeaway: Make bottlenecks visible before starting more work.

title: OKRs and SMART goals: connect ambition to outcomes
summary: Compare objectives and measurable key results with SMART criteria for defining clear goals.
takeaway: Describe the outcome you want and the evidence that will show progress.

title: Pareto: find the few factors with the greatest impact
summary: Explore the 80/20 heuristic with all the supplied individual, team and company examples.
takeaway: Investigate concentration in your own evidence; an exact 80/20 split is not a law.
notes: The final instruction in the source is incomplete (“with lower…”). It remains flagged as unfinished.
The relationships, health and investment examples are illustrations of the notes’ heuristic, not measured ratios or personalized advice.

title: Prioritization: urgency, scope, value and complexity
summary: Compare Eisenhower, MoSCoW and a value–complexity matrix for different prioritization questions.
takeaway: Choose the framework that matches the decision: time, delivery scope or implementation trade-off.
notes: The final value–complexity quadrant repeats low complexity. The visual marks low-value/high-complexity work as an editorial reconstruction, while retaining the original wording below.
MoSCoW’s “Won’t have” means outside the agreed timeframe, not necessarily excluded forever.

title: Feedback learning loops: coaching, team huddles and systemic change
summary: Turn customer signals into individual learning, shared problem solving and changes to recurring systems.
takeaway: Feedback becomes useful when someone acts on it and recurring issues reach the people who can change the system.

ranges.heading: Individual, team and systemic learning loops

notes: The source introduces these loops alongside NPS but supplies no prediction study or survey calculation. A loyalty measure alone does not prove business growth.
